author: José Saramago
introFa: کتاب «Blindness» نوشته José Saramago یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Blindness»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Psychol Res (1997) 60:173 182 © Springer-Verlag 1997 Bruce W. A. Whittlesea. Kwok H. Wai Reverse "repetition blindness" and release from "repetition blindness": Constructive variations on the "repetition blindness" effect Received: 26 June 1996/Accepted: 8 November 1996 Abstract N. Kanwisher observed that subjects shown rapid lists of words recall two occurrences of a repeated word less often than two unrelated words. Kanwisher explained this "repetition blindness" through a type/ token account, which assumes that encoding the second occurrence of a repeated word is inhibited if it occurs too soon after the first. More fundamentally, it assumes that failure to recall a word from a rapid list results from failure to encode its occurrence. Contrary to that inter- pretation, we observed that subjects can often recognize words that they cannot recall from a rapid list. We also observed "reverse repetition blindness," when the sec- ond presentation was given greater contextual support, and a "release from repetition blindness" effect, when distinctive contextual support was given to each occur- rence. We concluded that a constructive account of re- membering provides a better explanation of all of the effects. Introduction Kanwisher (e.g., 1987; Kanwisher & Potter, 1989, 1990) showed subjects lists of words that formed sentences, using rapid serial presentation. Some sentences con- tained a repeated word (e.g., "When she spilled the ink there was ink all over."); some contained a different but related word in place of one of the occurrences of the repeated word (e.g., "When she spilled the liquid there was ink all over."). Kanwisher observed that subjects reported both occurrences of the repeated word less often than they reported both of the two related words, an effect she called "repetition blindness." Moreover, when subjects reported only one occurrence of the re- B. W. A. Whittlesea ([]) Department of Psychology, Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, B.C., Canada V5A 1S6; e-mail: bruce_whittlesea@sfu.ca K. H. Wai Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, B.C., Canada peated word, they usually reported it selectively in the first location in which that word had been shown. Kanwisher concluded that subjects can usually report the first occurrence of a repeated word in a rapid list, but selectively fail to report the second. To explain this effect, Kanwisher (e.g., 1987; Park & Kanwisher, 1994) invoked a distinction between "type" and "token" representations of experience (cf. Anderson & Bower, 1973). According to this account, each object that a person encounters is identified as an example of some concept (its type) and is also individuated as a particular occurrence of that type: A token is formed to represent that particular occurrence. If subjects are shown a list of words, they can later report the list by reading out the set of types for which tokens were formed during the list. Applying this idea to the "repe- tition blindness" effect, Kanwisher concluded that the selective failure to report the second occurrence of a repeated word meant that formation of a token repre- senting the second occurrence is inhibited when it occurs too soon after the first. However, adopting that conclusion requires one to accept that there is a real distinction between two forms of memory, one for concepts and one for events (cf. Tulving, 1983, 1995). In a pair of articles, Whittlesea, Dorken, and Podrouzek (1995) and Whittlesea and Podrouzek (1995) argued against this conclusion, on both theoretical and procedural grounds. First, they argued that a report of a repeated word only in the first location in which that word was shown does not nec- essarily mean that the subject is reporting the first oc- currence of the word; instead, the subject could be reporting the second occurrence in the first location. The idea was that if a subject is shown a rapid list of words such as "The yellow car passed our car on the left" and fails to encode the first occurrence of the word "car," the subject is still likely to report "The yellow car passed our on the left" rather than "The yellow passed our car on the left." The reason is that reporting the repeated word only in the first location creates a largely comprehensible sentence, whereas reporting it only in the second pro-

174 duces a less understandable utterance. Moreover, the first version corresponds more closely to the rules of English syntax, which require that a concept mentioned twice in a sentence be referred to directly (by a noun) in the first instance, although a pronoun may be used in the second instance (e.g., "The yellow car passed ours" rather than "The yellow one passed our car"). Thus, if subjects are sensitive to the meaning of the utterance they report and to the rules of syntax, they are likely to report that word in the first location that it is required, even if they perceived it only in the second. Second, Whittlesea and Podrouzek (1995) argued that failure to report an occurrence of a word after the list does not necessarily mean that occurrence was not encoded (cf. Armstrong & Mewhort, 1995). Instead, it may mean that the occurrence is represented in memory, but that at test the subject lacks appropriate cues to retrieve that word. For example, a subject who is shown the sentence "After the wet spring the red roses faded" may have encoded the word "spring," but in reporting the sentence first recalls "the red roses faded." This proposition is a poor cue for retrieval of "spring," be- cause the idea of fading is more meaningfully associated with autumn than spring. In contrast, if the subject succeeded in reporting "After the wet," he or she would have a better cue to produce the word "spring," both because those words make sense of "spring" and be- cause "spring" is probably encoded as a component of the phrase containing those other words. The idea is that each word in a to-be-remembered sentence serves as a cue to retrieve its neighbors, and so does the emerging theme and syntax of the sentence: remembering a word is not dependent just on the existence of a representation of the occurrence of that word during the sentence, but also on interdependent encoding of words with their contexts and on hunches about what word ought to be in a particular location, given what meaning can be re- trieved and the rules of syntax. In consequence, failure to report a word may reflect a failure to produce effec- tive retrieval cues at rest, rather than failure to encode the word while the list was presented. These arguments are based on the idea that remem- bering is a reconstructive activity, rather than a read-out of active memory traces. In the act of remembering, people use knowledge about context (including syntax and meaning) as cues to generate further mental events, which are then reported as remembrances. This idea is clearly valid in long-term remembering: given a para- graph to read one day and tested a week later, people remember the theme and reconstruct the detail and specific wording around that theme, resulting in errors of omission and intrusion (e.g., Bartlett, 1932). The question is whether this principle of reconstruction is also valid in reporting events that occurred in the im- mediate past. Kanwisher's (1987) conclusion that failure to recall an occurrence of a word in a sentence results from failure to encode it rather than from a failure of reconstruction argues that remembering works differ- ently in immediate test than in the long term. Essentially, Kanwisher's (1987; Park & Kanwisher, 1994) interpretation treats the problem of reporting words from rapidly presented lists as one of detection, analogous to the problem faced by the subject in a sig- nal-detection experiment involving lights flashed near the threshold of perception. Under this analogy, it seems clear that sensitivity to the occurrence of a target word will depend primarily on registration of that occurrence in memory: the possession of a trace of the word, like the additional neural activity accompanying a light flash, is a necessary and sufficient basis for discriminating oc- currences from non-occurrences. Selective failure to re- port repeated words in the second location in which they are presented (relative to non-repeated words in the same location) thus indicates insensitivity to those oc- currences and argues for some mechanism preventing the encoding of repeated occurrences. In contrast, we treat reporting the list as a problem of remembering, even though the words to be reported were presented within the last few seconds. We therefore expect that successful report depends not only on encoding the word when it is presented in the list, but also on the same retrieval factors that control remembering in the longer term, including constructive processing and cue-depen- dent retrieval and forgetting~ We argue that selective report of repeated words in one presentation location or another reflects the operation of reconstructive activities performed after the list, in the act of recalling it. The experiments of this article are designed to illus- trate these reconstructive aspects of remembering in re- porting short, rapid lists. The first experiment demonstrates that failure to recall a word from a rapid list does not mean that the subjects failed to encode that occurrence of the word, because it can still be remem- bered if an appropriate cue is supplied. This finding undercuts claims that failure to recall a repeated word twice indicates that one of its occurrences was not en- coded. The second study presents a "reverse repetition blindness" effect, in which subjects have difficulty re- porting repeated words in the first location in which they occur, but no difficulty reporting them in the second; this effect is obtained by providing semantic and syntactic support for report in the second presentation location rather than the first. It demonstrates that there is no intrinsic tendency to report a repeated word in its first presentation location, and that instead, the location at which subjects report a repeated word depends on which occurrence has the greater contextual support. This finding contradicts the conclusion that the location of report can be taken as an index of which occurrence of a repeated word the subjects reported when they report only one occurrence. The third experiment shows a new effect, "release from repetition blindness," consisting of the observation that subjects have much less difficulty in reporting a repeated word twice if the occurrences are presented in distinctive contexts. This observation demonstrates that the occurrence of the "repetition blindness" effect results as much from poor retrieval conditions as it does from the rate of presentation of

175 stimuli. We interpret the results of these experiments as support for the conclusion drawn by Whittlesea et al. (1995) and Whittlesea and Podrouzek (1995) that "rep- etition blindness" is a problem of remembering repeti- tions, rather than a problem of encoding the second occurrence of a repeated item. Experiment 1: Evidence about recall as a measure of failure of encoding The type/token account of "repetition blindness" is based on the idea that failure to report a repeated word in the second location in which it was presented means that the subject failed to encode the second occurrence of that word as an actual event. This conclusion relies on the assumption that failure to recall an occurrence of a word can be taken as an indication that occurrence was not encoded. In the general literature on remembering, failure of recall is not ordinarily considered to be an indication that the subject failed to encode the item (cf. Tulving & Psotka, 1971), because free recall is notori- ously an ineffective method of remembering. However, if a subject were shown only one word, presented briefly, and could not report it immediately afterward, that failure would probably be justly interpreted as failure to encode the item well enough to report it. Given that subjects in Kanwisher's experiments were shown very short and rapid lists, with report following immediately after the list, the assumption that failure to recall indi- cates failure to encode is at least plausible. To test this assumption, we showed subjects short sentences, presented in rapid serial format. None of these sentences contained a repetition. However, each sentence contained two target words, one presented in a context that was appropriate in syntax and meaning, and the other presented in an inappropriate context. As an example, one of the sentences was "He went to TREE buy a LOAF of bread." In this sentence, the target words are "TREE" and "LOAF"; the latter fits its context, whereas the former is clearly in an anomalous context. Following each presentation, we tested subjects' knowledge of the sentence twice, once in a free recall test and then again in a recognition test. The logic was that if failure to recall a word following a rapid presentation means that the subject failed to encode that word, then subjects should be at chance in the recognition test when they had failed to recall a target word. Method the anomalous word (in early or late position) was counterbalanced across subjects. Trials were subject-placed. On each trial, subjects received a sentence, presented as a rapid serial list, and were then tested twice, once through recall and once through recognition. Each sentence was preceded by the word "READY," centered on the screen. On a keypress by the subject, the word was replaced by a fixation cross, again centered on the screen. The cross persisted for 250 ms. The sentences were then presented on a monitor, one word at a time, each centered on the screen, at 7 ticks (approximately 117 ms) per word, with no inter-stimulus interval. All words were presented in upper case, using a 12-point Monaco font. Viewing distance was about .4 m. Following the last word, a mask of ampersands was presented, longer than the longest word used, and again centered on the screen. Immediately after this presentation, the subject was required to recall the entire sentence. This recall was recorded on audiotape; we scored recall of the two target words. In all sentences, the anom- alous word was the same part of speech and the same length as the other target word. On each trial, following the recall test, the subject was shown two pairs of words. One pair contained the anomalous target word and a second word that had not been shown in the sentence, but was of the same part of speech and same length as the anomalous target: the other pair contained the other target word and yet an- other word that had not been in the list, again equated for length and part of speech. These pairs were presented in random order, and the sequence within a pair (old or new item on the left or right) was also randomized. The subject was required to guess which word of each pair had been presented in the list. Chance perfor- mance on the recognition test was therefore 50% accuracy. Rec- ognition accuracy was scored for each type of target. In addition, we isolated those trials on which subjects failed to recall target words presented in an anomalous context, and computed the ac- curacy of recognition for those trials separately. This procedure was not performed for words presented in appropriate contexts, because the rate of recalling those words was very high (greater than 80%), leaving few trials to compute a conditional recognition score. Results and discussion As can be seen in the top row of Table 1, subjects re- called many more words presented in appropriate loca- tions than words presented in anomalous contexts, t(13) = 5.44, p < .001. The question was whether this failure to recall the latter words resulted from failure to encode those words in a usable way, or failure to retrieve them later. As can be seen in the bottom row of Table 1, subjects claimed to recognize both kinds of target words more often than they could recall them. Of course, recall and recognition have different base rates and are not directly comparable. The critical comparison involves recogni- tion on the 49% of trials on which subjects had failed to recall the anomalous target. On those trials, subjects Subjects. Fourteen Simon Fraser University students participated for course credit. Procedure. We constructed 48 sentences, each of which contained two target words. One target fit its context in both meaning and syntax; the other was anomalous for its context (e.g., "They have six DAYS to DOOR complete the job"). Subjects were made aware that all sentences contained an anomalous word. The location, of Table 1 Exp. 1: Probability of recalling or claiming to recognize target words as a function of appropriateness of presentation context Appropriate context Anomalous context Recall test .80 .51 Recognition test .97 .83

176 achieved 68.1% accuracy in recognition, reliably above the chance rate (50%), t(13) = 4.94, p < .001. Clearly, the subjects were often able to recognize the anomalous words, indicating that they must have encoded them, even when they were unable to report those words in the recall test. This of course does not mean that recognition is a perfect index of encoding: Instead, it demonstrates that recall is a very poor indicator of whether or not a subject has encoded the occurrence of a word in a rapid list. The reason why anomalous targets were not recalled as often as the other targets seems clear. The former do not fit their contexts in either meaning or syntax. In recalling the sentence, the subject is guided by the global meaning of the sentence as a whole and by local orga- nization within phrases. That is, they reconstruct the details of the sentence based on what they can recall about its general properties. Targets in appropriate lo- cations benefit from this reconstructive process: Having recalled the context of a word, the subject is aware that some concept is required at that syntactic location and is cued to retrieve that particular word by the local meaning of the context. Lacking this contextual support, the anomalous words are often not recalled. However, the recognition task provides a more specific cue to re- member those words, namely the identity of that word itself, resulting in successful remembering. We therefore concluded that recognition is a more sensitive measure of the existence of a representation of an experience than is recall. This conclusion is obviously not new: it has existed at least since Tulving and Thompson's (1973)investigation. However, the present experiment demonstrates that recall is a poor measure of the existence of a representation even when the set of items to be recalled is small and the recall is performed within seconds of the presentation. Of course, the words that subjects failed to recall and later recognized in this experiment were not repeated words. However, the anomalous target words were presented in disadvanta- geous contexts for recall, just as (we argue) second oc- currences of repeated words in a sentence are presented in a syntactic context that is disadvantageous for report. The logic of using recall as an index of failure to encode once-presented items applies equally in making infer- ences about the encoding of twice-presented words. We conclude that failure to recall a repeated word in its second presentation location does not necessarily indi- cate failure to establish a representation of the second occurrence of that word. Experiment 2: Reverse "repetition blindness" The type/token account of "repetition blindness" re- quires that if encoding of one of two occurrences of a repeated word is inhibited, it must be the second oc- currence. This is required logically, because encoding of a later item could not prevent the encoding of an earlier item that has already taken place. Thus if under some condition subjects regularly report repeated items in the second presentation location but not the first, the ac- count would be in some difficulty. In this experiment, we presented repeated words in sentences such as "The diamond ring GIFT was a GIFT from his heart." In these sentences, the first occurrence of the repeated word was presented in a location in which it fit neither syntactically nor in terms of the sense of the sentence. Control sentences were similar, except that they replaced the first occurrence of the repetition with an unrelated word, for example "The diamond ring SOCK was a GIFT from his heart." The previous experiment demonstrates that words presented in anomalous loca- tions of the sentence were difficult to recall, but are nonetheless usually encoded. Thus, if the type/token ac- count of the "repetition blindness" effect is correct, pre- sentation of the first occurrence of a repeated word should often inhibit encoding of the second occurrence, even if the first occurrence is not later recallable. In consequence, we should observe that subjects report both occurrences of a repeated word less often than the two occurrences of unrelated words. We should also observe that repeated words are reported less often in the second response lo- cation than nonrepeated targets, because encoding the second occurrences of repeated words would be selec- tively inhibited. We should definitely not observe that repeated words are reported more often in the second location than nonrepeated words when the subject re- ports only one word, but that is what happened. Method Subjects. Sixteen Simon Fraser University students participated for course credit. Procedure. We constructed 48 sentences, each containing an anomalous word that did not fit its context either in meaning or syntax. Subjects were made aware that all sentences contained an anomalous word, but told that they were to report that word along with the others. In half of these sentences, that anomalous word did not occur again later in the sentence (e.g., "He poured some blue ink TAX into a JAR yesterday"), and in half it did (e.g., "He poured some blue ink JAR into a JAR yesterday"). As demon- strated by these examples, lag between target items was equated between repeated and nonrepeated sentences. Between subjects, sentences were switched from one condition to the other by sub- stituting a repeated word in the first target location for a nonre- peated one, or vice versa. 1Downing and Kanwisher (1995) argued that the second occur- rence may sometimes be individuated, and the first occurrence not encoded: for example, when the instructions emphasize report of the end of a sentence, or the second occurrence is presented as a picture. This argument seems to stretch the account rather far. Because the first occurrence would have been individuated if the second occurrence were not presented in the list and is reportable when a second occurrence is not presented, there must be some representation formed on the first, at the time it is presented, that is maintained until inhibited by individuation of the second. How- ever, Downing and Kanwisher do not explain what form this representation is supposed to take, or how individuation of the second occurrence retroactively inhibits the already-formed repre- sentation of the first.

177 Trials were subject-paced. On each trial, subjects received a sentence, presented as a rapid serial list, and were then required to recall the entire list. The lists were presented on a monitor, at 117 ms per word, with no inter-stimulus interval. All words were presented in upper case, in 12-point Monaco font. Immediately after this presentation, the subject was required to recall the entire sentence. This recall was recorded on audiotape. We scored the subjects' success in reporting the two target items, whether repeated or not. The first eight trials were treated as practice and not scored. In this and the following experiment, we follow a convention established by Whittlesea et al. (1995) for labeling events of interest. Other investigators use a single code, such as "CI" and "C2," to denote the locations of first and second presentations of target words as well as the first and second locations in which items could be reported. However, we believe that use of this single code has created a subtle confusion in deducing the subjects' mental processing from their overt behavior. For example, saying "the subjects reported CI" means they produced a response in the first report location, but also implies that they reported the first presentation of the word. How- ever, as indicated earlier, we assume that subjects could be reporting the second occurrence of a repeated word in the first response lo- cation. To avoid confounding location of report with which pre- sentation was reported, we will employ the terms "P 1" and "P2" to denote first and second presentation locations, and "RI" and "R2" to denote first and second report locations. Results and discussion Results are presented in Table 2. As can be seen in the table (third column), the subjects suffered "repetition blindness", in that the probability of reporting both occurrences of a repeated word was less than the prob- ability of reporting both target unrelated words on a trial, t(15) = 2.93, p < .01. Examining columns 1 and 2, it is also clear that when subjects failed to report both occurrences of a repeated word, they selectively reported that word in R2 rather than R1. Columns 4 and 5 show this effect in a different way, demonstrating an overall selective deficit in reports of the repeated word in R1. This "reverse repetition blindness" effect makes no sense under the type/token account: To be explained through inhibition, it would require a later event to inhibit the encoding of an earlier event. 2 Instead, we interpret these results to show recon- structive processes at work in remembering the list. On those occasions when the subject reports a repeated word only once, he or she had to make a choice whether to report it in the first location where meaning and syntax demand it, leaving the second blank, or in the second, leaving the first blank. As discussed earlier, meaning and syntax are ordinarily better served by reporting the word in the first rather than the second location, and subjects usually follow that principle in reconstructing their ex- 2 The reader may be reminded of the "backwards masking effect," in which a stimulus presented immediately after another one appears to block encoding of the earlier item. However, in the case of '"repetition blindness," the "masking" stimulus is not presented immediately after the earlier target: instead, it is presented with a lag of at least one, and up to three, intervening words, which themselves are not "masked." The perceptual basis of the back- ward masking effect is thus not likely to be related to the "repetition blindness" effect. Table 2 Exp. 2: Probability of reporting repeated and nonrepeated words in first (R1) and second (R2) response locations Presentation Target occurrences reported in: R1 only R2 only Both R1 total R2 total Repeated .08 .76 .07 .15 .83 Nonrepeated .06 .58 .22 .28 .80 perience of the list. However, in the present experiment, we made the first occurrence anomalous: In this case, reporting the word in the first location and leaving it out of the second would produce nonsense, as for example, "The diamond ring gift was a from his heart." The sub- jects respond to the meaningful organization of the sen- tence and instead report the word only in the second location, producing the comprehensible sentence "The diamond ring was a gift from his heart." We argue that this reconstruction also explains why subjects ordinarily report repeated words selectively in the first location of normal sentences, because the first occurrence of a re- peated word is well supported by local syntax and meaning, and because English syntax requires that a concept repeated within a sentence be represented by a noun only once, on its first mention within a sentence. We conclude that report of rapid sentences should be thought of as a reconstructive activity, a process of deciding what words occurred and where they occurred, rather than detection and report of traces. There are a variety of ways of showing that subjects' reports of sentences are reconstructions rather than re- ports of tokens coded by location. For example, we could have shown subjects sentences like "The diamond ring gift was a from his heart," in which no repetition occurs, but the target word is in the wrong location syntactically and semantically. Predictably, people will rationalize that sentence in recall, reporting '°The dia- mond ring was a gift from his heart." Perhaps more forcing, one could set up sentences that required two reports of a single word and present that word only once, in either the first or the second occasion that syntax and meaning demand it: For example, "The yellow car passed our on the left" and "The yellow passed our car on the left." If report of a word in a particular location is controlled by a token that codes the position of that word during presentation, as re- quired by the type/token account, then subjects should be fairly accurate in reporting the target word where it was presented. However, if subjects generally reported the word "car" in the first target location and not in the second, regardless of where it was presented, that would provide strong evidence that the location of report was under the control of the subjects' knowledge of syntax and the meaning of the sentence, and that the report was a reconstruction of the experience rather than a veridical report. That experiment was conducted by Whittlesea et al. (1995, Exp. 1) and produced the latter result. Such erroneous reports of words in locations where they make sense, rather than in the locations at which

178 they were presented, also demonstrates the danger of interpreting which instance of a repeated word is re- ported from the location in which it is reported, as is usually done in experiments on repetition blindness. We do not argue that subjects in this experiment were ac- tually reporting the second instance of the repeated word when they reported the word in the second response location: They could as easily have been reporting the first instance in that location, guided by the demands of syntax and meaning (cf. Whittlesea et al., 1995). In fact, it seems likely to us that report of the word in the second location is not a selective report of either presentation, but instead is a production supported by representations of both occurrences. Experiment 3: Release from "repetition blindness" In this experiment, all words were presented in congru- ous contexts. For example, we presented words re- peatedly in sentences such as "Our blue boat is the biggest new boat in the harbor" and "We sleep at night and then sleep during the day." These sentences are similar to ones used by other investigators; for example, Kanwisher (1987) used sentences like ~We got into this van and another van for the commute," "It was work time so work had to get done," and "The brown couch and the black couch were stolen" (p. 145). In all these sentences, the contexts in which the repeated word oc- curred were different, but not distinctively so. We sus- pected that this might be a source of the subjects' difficulty in reporting both occurrences of the repeated word. If the subjects cannot remember distinctive in- formation about each separate occurrence of the word after the list, they are likely to think that it occurred in only one context and thus occurred only once (cf. Whittlesea et al., 1995). To test this idea, we constructed other sentences in which the two target words were presented in somewhat more elaborate or distinctive contexts. For example, we used sentences such as "When our boat sank the rescue boat saved our lives" and "We sleep in bed but dogs sleep on the floor." While not startling, these sentences present slightly more elaborate and distinctive contexts for the two occurrences of the target word than do the previous ones. The question was whether providing more distinctive contexts for the two occurrences of a repeated word would influence the size of the "repetition blindness" effect. Method Subjects. Twelve Simon Fraser University students participated for course credit in Exp. 3a, and 16 in Exp. 3b. Procedure. We created 48 sentences, across which repetition and distinctiveness of context were factorially combined. Sentences were constructed in frames of four, each sentence in the frame expressing one of the combinations of repetition and distinctive- ness. For example, one frame consisted of the four sentences: °°The teacher gave the test today and the test was easy" (repeated non- distinctive); "The teacher gave the quiz today and the test was easy" (nonrepeated nondistinctive); "He failed the history test but the math test was easy" (repeated distinctive); and "He failed the history quiz but the math test was easy" (nonrepeated distinctive). As illustrated by these examples, the total number of words in a sentence, the location of the P1 and P2 targets within the sentence, and the lag between targets were held constant across the sentences within a frame. Any particular subject received one of these four sentences; the next subject received a different one from this frame, and so on. There were thus four counterbalanced conditions, which were used equally often across subjects. Each subject received eight practice trials (which were not scored), and then ten trials of each of the four combinations of repetition and contextual distinctiveness. The difference between nondistinctive and distinctive contexts was subjective and is hard to describe. In general, we tried to make the nondistinctive sentences bland in meaning and/or make the second context refer to the same word as the first without adding much information, and tried to make the latter sentences somewhat more elaborate in meaning and/or more different in context. Some examples: °'He bought a tennis racquet and gave the racquet to the girl" (nondistinctive) versus "He hung his new racquet behind the tennis racket in the hall" (distinctive); "She picked up the glass and put the glass somewhere" versus "When she dropped the glass there was broken glass everywhere"; "The fire chief was the best chief they had met" versus "The fire chief met the police chief of the town"; "The little girls cried when the girls were in trouble" versus "The little girls cried when older girls laughed at them"; and "The yellow car passed the red car on the left" versus "The yellow car passed the sports car on the left." Clearly, the difference is not great: In general, the latter sentences were intended to give both occurrences a context that is somewhat more elaborate and distinctive than those in the former sentences. We tested whether the sentences actually differed in distinc- tiveness in a separate test (Exp. 3a). In this test, subjects were shown pairs of sentences typed on paper. Each member of a pair contained the same repeated word but differed in context (e.g., "She liked the picture although the picture was bad" and "She liked his picture but the picture frame broke"). Subjects were asked to read each pair and then to indicate in which sentence of the pair the two occurrences of the repeated word were presented more distinctively. They had unlimited time to perform this task. In the main experiment (3b), sentences were shown tachisto- scopically, in rapid serial format, and all four combinations of the factors (Distinctiveness x Repetition) were employed. Subjects were not informed that every sentence was grammatically complete. Instead, they were led to believe that some sentences might have a missing word. They were instructed to report exactly what they had seen, leaving the sentence grammatically incorrect if necessary. Trials were subject-paced. On each trial, subjects received a sentence presented as a rapid serial list and were then required to recall the entire list. The lists were presented on a monitor at 117 ms per word, with no inter-stimulus interval. All words were presented in upper case. Immediately after this presentation, sub- jects were required to recall the entire sentence. We scored the subjects' success in reporting the two target items, whether repeated or not. In this experiment, subjects were required to report the lists on paper. After each sentence was presented, subjects were given a re- port protocol. The protocol contained the first and last word of the sentence, and also a word that occurred between the two target items, with blanks between words long enough to write the missing words. For example, the protocol for the sentence "The teacher gave the test today and the test was easy" was "The and easy." This protocol made scoring more accurate than was possible with audio-recording. It does not differentially provide recall cues for repeated versus nonrepeated trials; in fact, the same protocol was used in both cases. The protocol for the parallel distinctive sentence ("He failed the history test but the math test was easy") would be "He _ _ but _ _ easy."

179 Results and discussion Distinctiveness is a subjective attribute: The same stim- ulus can be experienced as either distinctive or nondis- tinctive by different people, depending on their prior experiences and current understanding. Moreover, when using sentences in which a word is repeated at lag three or less, there are severe limitations on how distinctive the two contexts of the word can be. Experiment 3a was a manipulation check designed to evaluate whether the sentences that we intended to contain more distinctive contexts were generally experienced that way by our subjects. We observed considerable variability in the subjects' judgements about which item of each pair provided more distinctive contexts for the repeated word. Even sentence pairs such as "The worst smells were the bad smells from the garbage" (meant to be nondistinctive) and "Rotten garbage smells bad but perfume smells sweet all day" (meant to be distinctive) did not achieve completely consistent ratings from our subjects. How- ever, despite this variability, on average the subjects chose the alternatives that we intended to be more dis- tinctive on 76% of trials, SE = 2.7%, reliably above chance of 50%, t(11) = 9.63, p < .01. We concluded that our intended manipulation of distinctive versus nondis- tinctive contexts was not powerful or completely con- sistent, but that, taken as a whole, the set of sentences that we meant to be more distinctive were experienced as such by the subjects. If distinctiveness of context is im- portant in reporting repeated words from rapidly pre- sented sentences, we could thus expect to observe some effect of our manipulation. This prediction was tested in Exp. 3b. As can be seen in the first two rows of Table 3, we observed the usual "repetition blindness" effect when the contexts were nondistinctive: Subjects were 25% less likely to report both occurrences of a repeated word than both nonrepeated targets in a sentence, and when subjects failed to report a repeated word twice, they usually reported that word in R1 only. This is the pattern commonly observed in studies of "repetition blindness" using sentences (e.g., Kanwisher, 1987; Kanwisher & Potter, 1989, 1990). The situation changed radically when we provided distinctive contexts (rows three and four of Table 3). Providing distinctive contexts increased the probability of reporting both occurrences of the repeated word from .52 to .67, F(1,15) = 7.73, MSE= .022, p < .014. However, the distinctive contexts did not reliably affect the probability of reporting both nonrepeated targets, which increased only from .77 to .79, F(1, 15)= 0.43, MSE -- .007, p < .523. In consequence, the magnitude of the "repetition blindness" effect was greatly reduced, from (.77 - .52 =) 25% with nondistinctive contexts to (.79- .67 =) 12% with distinctive contexts. 3 We con- cluded that providing distinctive contexts selectively in- creased the probability of reporting repeated words twice. It is difficult to see how this "release from repetition blindness" effect can be explained through the type/to- ken account. According to this account, "repetition blindness" results from a refractory period for attaching a token to a type: When a second occurrence of a word occurs within a critical period after the first, the first occurrence will be tokenized, but the second will not. However, the two conditions of this experiment (dis- tinctive and nondistinctive contexts) had identical tem- poral parameters: Duration of presentations was held constant, and lag between items was equated between conditions. It is no part of the type/token account that the contexts must be nondistinctive for tokenization to be inhibited, or that distinctive contexts can cancel the inhibition of tokenization. Instead, we interpreted the effect of distinctive con- texts on report of repeated items through a reconstruc- tive perspective. We suggest that the nonrepeated words did not benefit from the context manipulation because, being different words, they were already distinctive: Having these two words come to mind after the trial would assure the subjects that they had perceived two different events and permit them to report both. In contrast, even if both occurrences of the repeated word were encoded and both occurrences sponsored remem- bering after the list, that would cause only one thing to come to mind, namely, the identity of the word. To know that the word occurred twice, the subjects would need some indication that they had seen it on two dif- ferent occasions. Having the word come to mind in two distinct contexts could permit the subjects to decide that they had seen it twice. A related possibility is that the distinctive contexts freed subjects to some extent from the syntactic rule against repeating a word in a sentence. For example, it simply sounds redundant to say "The red car passed the blue car on the left": One ought to use a pronoun in place of the second occurrence of "car." The subjects' bias is therefore not to report the word a second time unless they have clear evidence that it occurred again. 3The "repetition blindness" effect was still greater than chance in the distinctive condition, t(15)= 2.84, p < .013. The fact that "repetition blindness" was not reduced to zero is not surprising. First, as indicated earlier, the manipulation of the distinctiveness of the two contexts was not powerful. Second, on some occasions subjects could not report the context of one or both of the targets. This would not affect report of nonrepeated items: because they are already different in identity, they do not require contextual support to be reported as different occurrences. However, failure to report both contexts would prevent the "distinctiveness" manipulation from taking effect on repeated trials. Third, the general syntactic rule not to report a word twice in a sentence still obtains. Even in our "distinctive" case, with sentences like "He hung his new racquet behind the tennis racquet in the hall," it is easy and perhaps more usual to replace the second occurrence of the repeated noun with a pronoun, saying "He hung his new racquet behind the one in the hall." The greater distinctiveness relaxes the bias against saying a word twice, but does not necessarily eliminate it. We concluded that the reduction of the "repetition blindness" effect by half, against all of these factors, was impressive.

180 Table 3 Exp. 3: Probability of reporting repeated and non- repeated words in first (R1) and second (R2) response location, as a function of distinctiveness of the separate contexts Presentation Target occurrences reported in: R1 only R2 only Both R1 total R2 total Non-distinctive contexts: Repeated Nonrepeated Distinctive contexts: Repeated Nonrepeated .45 .03 .52 .97 .55 .19 .02 .77 .96 .79 .26 .07 .67 .93 .74 .18 .04 .79 .97 .83 However, when the contexts are more distinctive, re- peated use of the word may actually be encouraged: For example, the double use of "car" in "The red car passed the stolen car on the left" may actually be preferable to the use of the pronoun in the second location. In that case, the difference in context relaxes the bias against reporting the word twice. However, if this is the source of the "release from repetition blindness" effect, it im- plies that the "repetition blindness" effect itself results from obeying an injunction against using words re- peatedly in simple sentences, rather than from some hypothetical inhibition of encoding. The decision not to report a word twice in a sentence or, alternatively, to report it twice, on grounds of syntactic rules, is an ex- ample of one of the ways in which reconstructive pro- cesses after the list can determine what subjects report. The "release from proactive interference" effect (e.g., Wickens, 1973), after which our effect was named, demonstrates that subjects have difficulty in reporting words belonging to the same category, but that a shift in category permits subjects to recall without interference. The effect could mean that succeeding items that belong in the same category as earlier items are not encoded well. However, Gardiner, Craik, and Birtwhistle (1972) demonstrated that the release effect can occur even if the shift in category is not made plain to subjects until after they have encoded the list and are about to report it: The subjects' awareness that the items they are to report come from a different category than preceding items permits them to make more useful report decisions after the list. This result clearly indicates that the interference resulting from categorical similarity is caused by a problem in how to think about the list during the recall phase, not by a problem of encoding the items at the time they are presented. Although by no means exact, we suggest that there is a parallel between the problems associated with report- ing two identical items from a short list and those of reporting items from the same category on succeeding trials. Subjects in the proactive interference studies have an increasingly difficult job of deciding whether the word that comes to mind now came from the current list or a prior list. Changing the category provides a selective cue for recall of items of the new category and assures the subject that any word that now comes to mind in that category should be reported. Similarly, subjects in a °'repetition blindness" study, having already reported a word once, require extra evidence to report it a second time. Making the contexts distinctive serves to break the sentence into distinct events or meaning units. The dis- tinctive contexts serve as selective cues for recall of each specific event and allow the subject to report the word a second time, not as a repetition, but as a component of a clearly different event. Just as providing a new category removes the subjects' uncertainty about whether a word now in mind comes from the present list or a previous one, providing distinctive contexts changes the subjects' task from deciding whether a word occurred twice to deciding what words occurred in each meaning unit of the sentence. Failure to report both occurrences when the contexts are nondistinctive does not indicate that subjects failed to encode one of the occurrences. Instead, it simply indicates that nondistinctive contexts provide a poor basis for deciding that a word occurred twice, even when both contexts are remembered after the list, just as providing the same category as a cue for successive re- sponses produces proactive interference, without causing an encoding deficit. General discussion Together, the experiments of this article demonstrate that reporting words presented in rapid lists is far more variable than one would expect if it was primarily de- pendent on the formation or inhibition of token repre- sentations. The probability of remembering any word depends on how it is tested (Exp. 1). The location at which a repeated word is reported depends on the se- mantic and syntactic support of the contexts available at each report location, rather than the location at which the word is first presented (Exp. 2). The probability of reporting a repeated word twice is not determined by the rate of presentation alone but instead can be largely modified by the distinctiveness of the two contexts (Exp. 3). We concluded that the type/token theory of representation is inadequate to explain the variations in effects that can be obtained in report of rapid lists. In- stead, we concluded that these effects can be explained more easily by assuming that remembering is a con- structive activity, consisting of decisions about what the past must have been. Instead of simply retrieving and reporting representations of earlier events, people actu- ally reconstruct their experience after the list, attempting

181 to create a coherent whole, organizing and interpreting whatever fragments of experience currently come to mind. Most of the work on the "repetition blindness" effect has used lists of unrelated words rather than sentences (e.g., Park and Kanwisher, 1994; Bavelier & Potter, 1992). In that case, one might expect that the recon- structive effects demonstrated in this article would be irrelevant, because these lists have no overall meaning or general coherence that could guide later reconstructive processes. However, Armstrong and Mewhort (1995) showed that subjects have less difficulty in reporting the second occurrence of a repeated letter presented in a list of unrelated letters if they are first shown the specific context in which that word occurred during the list. Similarly, Whittlesea and Podrouzek (1995) demon- strated that reporting the occurrence of repetition in a list of unrelated words is greatly affected by other ac- tivities that the subject performs after the list, prior to deciding about the repetition. For example, subjects were much more likely to report that repetition had occurred within the list when shown the repeated word after the list or asked to recall the list prior to making their decision. Masson, Caldwell, and Whittlesea (1996) showed that constructive processes can influence recall even when the two targets are not identical but instead are orthographically related. For example, when shown a list containing two words like COOK and CORK, subjects usually reported the first but often failed to report the second, just as in the "repetition blindness" effect. However, when the list also contained a context word (e.g., WINE) that was related to the second word, the probability of reporting the second word increased considerably. Like the context effects of the experiments of this article, these effects demonstrate that success in report- ing words from rapid lists is not a consequence of simply forming or failing to form a token representing the oc- currence of the word, but instead results from an inter- action between the representations formed when the list is presented and the activities performed after the list, in the attempt to recall. We conclude that reconstructing one's experiences of the past in the act of recall is a very general phenomenon, occurring not only when the events are long past, but also in the very short term, even when the events to be reported occurred within the last couple of seconds. Fundamentally, this conclusion calls into question the relationship between remembering and experience. The type/token account is based on the idea that re- membering is direct report of experience, through the formation and retrieval of representations of events. Similar ideas have been proposed by other investigators. For example, Mandler (1980) proposed that the feeling of familiarity is a direct product of the activation of a memory trace by a stimulus in the environment. In contradiction of this idea, numerous investigators have demonstrated that the feeling of familiarity for a stim- ulus event can occur in the absence of a prior experience of that event (cf. Jacoby, Kelley, & Dywan, 1989, for a review). Instead, the feeling of familiarity appears to be the product of an unconscious decision that the subject makes about the source of their current fluency in dealing with a stimulus. For example, Whittlesea (1993) showed subjects a rapid list of words and then required them to judge whether a target word was in the list. This target word was presented in a sentence, such as "The stormy seas tossed the BOAT." Unknown to subjects, the sentences were of two types. One led the subject to expect the terminal (target) word to some degree, as in the example just given; the other did not (e.g., "She saved her money and bought a BOAT"). When only trials on which the word had not been presented in the list were examined, so that the possibility of true re- membering did not arise and only a feeling of familiarity could sway their judgment, subjects were 104 ms. faster in identifying the target in the former kind of sentence than the latter. They were also 19% likelier to judge that the word had been in the list when it was in a predictive context than when it was not. These subjects suffered an illusion of having seen the target item in the list, based on experiencing unexpected fluency in the predictive sentences. Such illusions may be rare; in general, when one experiences unexpected fluency in dealing with a stimulus, it may be quite correctly attributed to an in- fluence of past experience. However, the occurrence of the illusion demonstrates that the feeling of familiarity, the essential feeling of remembering, is itself not a direct product of the possession of a memory trace, but instead the product of a decision process that attributes the fluency of current processing to a source in the past. People are always in an uncertain relation to their past. Experience creates changes in memory; these changes produce differences in performance and make ideas come to mind when one encounters a stimulus. In the case of nonreflective performance, such as identify- ing objects or behaving appropriately toward them, the person has little problem. For example, when one sees a dog, the name "dog" comes to mind. This occurrence is sponsored by thousands of prior experiences and runs off fluently. However, the goal in remembering is not to use a mental event to act on the present world but to specify the source in the past that is responsible for the occurrence of that mental event; that is, to work back- ward from product to source. However, mental events are not isomorphic with the sources in memory that produce them. There are multiple sources of influence in the past, and any given mental event may have been produced in many ways. If the image of a dog comes to mind, one can expect the occurrence to be the product of prior experience, but is it the product of a single prior experience of seeing that dog, or multiple experiences of that dog, or even a composite of multiple dogs seen previously? The problem is that memory only places products in consciousness. The processes by which they are created, and the sources that these processes operate on, remain inaccessible. The person can only answer questions about the source of current mental events in-

182 ferentially, on the basis of a decision process like "I would have this idea now if the past was like that: therefore, I will decide that the past was like that." People are thus always in the position of evaluating their current performance as evidence about what their past must have been. They have no direct access to their past: They can only reconstruct it, using heuristics about the usual effects of certain kinds of past experience. This is the fundamental basis of the "repetition blindness" effect in rapid list presentation. The only way people can decide that they saw a word twice is if they can recall seeing the word in two different contexts; recalling it in one context only reassures them that they saw it at all. In contrast, to decide that they saw a word once and report it once only requires that word come to mind after the list with some feeling of familiarity. In consequence, the subjects can decide that they saw two separate target words, and report them both, more easily than they can decide they saw one word twice, and report it twice. We believe that this difference in the amount of evidence needed to decide if one saw a word twice is the source of the "repetition blindness" effect.
